title: A hypothetical two person California corporation is asked for a workers compensation certificate and reads the statutes on who must be covered
label: hypothetical
labelNote: This is a hypothetical built only to walk through California Labor Code sections 3700 and 3352 and the Division of Workers' Compensation employer FAQ; no real business, policy, premium, waiver, audit, or claim is described, and it is not a compliance opinion or a legal opinion for anyone.
whatHappened: In the hypothetical, two people form a California corporation. Both are officers and members of the board, they own all of the stock between them, and the corporation has no other workers, no payroll to anyone else, and no subcontractors. A general contractor they want to work for asks for a certificate of workers compensation insurance. The corporation wants to understand what California law says about who must be covered and about the officer exclusion [S:lab-3700] [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs] [S:lab-3352]. The business, the owners, and the certificate request are invented; the statutes and the agency guidance are real.
informationThatMattered: Labor Code section 3700 provides that every employer except the state shall secure the payment of compensation in one or more of the listed ways, including insuring with one or more insurers duly authorized to write compensation insurance in California or obtaining a certificate of consent to self-insure from the Director of Industrial Relations [S:lab-3700].
The Division of Workers' Compensation states that all California employers must provide workers' compensation benefits to their employees under Labor Code section 3700 [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs].

The Division states that executive officers and directors of corporations must be included in workers' compensation coverage unless the corporation is fully owned by the directors and officers, in which case they may elect to be excluded from workers' compensation benefits [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs].

Labor Code section 3352 sets the conditions for the officer and director exclusion: ownership of at least 10 percent of the issued and outstanding stock, or at least 1 percent where a listed family member owns at least 10 percent, coverage by a health insurance policy or health care service plan, and a written waiver of rights under the chapter executed under penalty of perjury [S:lab-3352].

Under section 3352 the waiver is effective upon the date of receipt and acceptance by the corporation's insurance carrier, the carrier may backdate acceptance up to 15 days, and a sole shareholder officer or director is excluded unless an election is made under section 4151(a) [S:lab-3352].

In the hypothetical, the certificate is being requested by a general contractor as part of its own contracting arrangements; the sources read here describe the Labor Code and the Division's guidance and say nothing about that contractor's requirements.
insuranceQuestion: What do the Labor Code and the Division of Workers' Compensation say about whether a corporation owned entirely by its two officer directors must carry workers compensation coverage, and about excluding those officers?
reasoningPath:
The starting rule is broad. Section 3700 provides that every employer except the state shall secure the payment of compensation in one or more of the listed ways, which include insuring with an authorized compensation insurer and obtaining a certificate of consent to self-insure from the Director of Industrial Relations [S:lab-3700]. The Division of Workers' Compensation states the same duty plainly: all California employers must provide workers' compensation benefits to their employees under section 3700 [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs]. Whether these two officers are employees for this purpose is therefore the question the statutes turn on, and it is a legal question for a lawyer or for the Division rather than one this page answers.

Officers are the wrinkle. The Division states that executive officers and directors of corporations must be included in coverage unless the corporation is fully owned by the directors and officers, and that where the directors and officers fully own the corporation they may elect to be excluded from workers' compensation benefits [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs]. That is why full ownership by the officers is the fact the hypothetical is built around, and why a corporation with outside shareholders is a different situation under that same guidance.

The mechanics of the election live in section 3352 and they are specific. The exclusion for an officer or member of the board requires ownership of at least 10 percent of the issued and outstanding stock, or at least 1 percent where a listed family member owns at least 10 percent, coverage by a health insurance policy or health care service plan, and a written waiver of rights under the chapter executed under penalty of perjury [S:lab-3352]. The waiver is effective upon receipt and acceptance by the corporation's insurance carrier, and the carrier may backdate acceptance up to 15 days [S:lab-3352]. Section 3352 also treats a sole shareholder officer or director as excluded unless an election is made under section 4151(a) [S:lab-3352]. Because the waiver route is written to run through a carrier's acceptance, the paperwork and the coverage question are tied together.

The contract layer is separate from the statute and is often why the question comes up. A general contractor asking for a certificate is enforcing its own contracting arrangements. Satisfying the Labor Code and satisfying that contract are two different questions, and nothing here resolves either one. Adding workers can change the statutory analysis, and section 3352 is where the categories of persons who are and are not employees for this purpose are set out, including several exclusions with their own conditions [S:lab-3352].

The consequences of getting this wrong are published by the agency. The Division states that section 3700.5 makes operating without coverage a misdemeanor punishable by either a fine of not less than $10,000 or imprisonment in the county jail for up to one year, or both; that a stop order prohibits the use of employee labor until coverage is obtained, with failure to observe it a misdemeanor punishable by up to 60 days in county jail or a fine of up to $10,000, or both; and that penalties of up to $100,000 are issued against illegally uninsured employers [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs]. That is the reason to take this question to counsel or to the Division rather than to infer an answer from an article.
decidedBy: No authority decided this. It is illustrative only. The statutes and the Division of Workers' Compensation guidance described are real; the corporation, the owners, and the certificate request are invented for the walkthrough.
cannotGeneralize: The Division's officer exclusion guidance turns on the corporation being fully owned by its directors and officers [S:dir-dwc-employer-faqs]. A different ownership structure is a different question under that same guidance.

Entity type matters. Section 3352 addresses officers and directors, general partners and managing members, owners of professional corporations, and officers and directors of cooperative corporations under separate provisions with different conditions [S:lab-3352].

This is general information about published statutes and agency guidance. It is not a compliance opinion, not a legal opinion, and not a determination that any business may or may not operate without coverage. That is a legal question for a lawyer, or a question for the Division of Workers' Compensation.
The sources read here do not address what any contract, licensing body, or certificate holder requires. Those requirements come from documents that were not read for this walkthrough.

Statutes and agency guidance change. Confirm the current text of sections 3700, 3352, and 4151 and the current Division of Workers' Compensation guidance before relying on the thresholds, procedures, and penalty amounts recorded here.
provenance: Hypothetical. No real client, business, policy, premium, waiver, audit, claim, quote, or placement outcome is described, and no carrier is named. The framework is drawn from California Labor Code sections 3700 and 3352 as displayed on California Legislative Information and from the California Division of Workers' Compensation employer frequently asked questions page, all fetched and read on 2026-08-31.
